projects.title: Tambayan — Social Media Platform
projects.tagline: A full-stack social media app built while learning Next.js
projects.description: Tambayan is a personal social media project created by Selwyn Rollorata while learning NextJs - follow the tutorial on YouTube: Codesistency. The project aims to provide a platform for users to connect, share content, and interact with each other in a user-friendly environment. It features user authentication, profile management, content posting, and real-time notifications.

caseStudy.context: Tambayan was born from a desire to learn modern full-stack web development. Following a guided tutorial, the project evolved into a fully functional social media platform where users can connect, share content, and interact in real-time.
caseStudy.challenge: Building a complete social media experience required mastering several interconnected technologies: server-side rendering with Next.js App Router, database design with Prisma and PostgreSQL, user authentication with Clerk, and file uploads with Uploadthing.
caseStudy.process: Following the guided tutorial by Codesistency (YouTube), I started by setting up the Next.js project with App Router architecture. Integrated Clerk for secure authentication, designed the database schema with Prisma ORM connected to PostgreSQL, and built features incrementally — from user profiles to content feeds to real-time notifications.
caseStudy.outcome: A fully deployed social media platform with user authentication, profile management, content posting, real-time notifications, and responsive design with both light and dark mode support. Deployed live on Vercel.
takeaways: Gained hands-on experience with Next.js App Router and Server Components
Learned database design and ORM usage with Prisma and PostgreSQL
Implemented secure authentication flows with Clerk
Built a responsive UI with light and dark mode support

projects.title: Mare — Brand Identity Redesign

caseStudy.context: Atty. Rema 'Mare' needed a refreshed brand identity that reflected professionalism while maintaining approachability. The existing logo felt dated and lacked versatility across digital and print media.
caseStudy.challenge: Creating a logo that balances the gravitas of a legal professional with a warm, approachable personality. The design needed to work across various formats — social media, print materials, and digital platforms — while being distinct and memorable.

takeaways: Learned to balance client personality with professional industry expectations
Developed a systematic approach to brand identity with color palettes and variants
Practiced iterative design with before/after comparison documentation

projects.title: Gemida Family — Heritage Web App
projects.tagline: A family management and genealogy platform built with Next.js and AI tools
projects.description: A family management and visualization web app built with Next.js (App Router). It provides user authentication, family tree visualization and management, event & timeline features, image uploads, and an admin interface for the Gemida Family - Kaliwat ni Cresenciano ug Ricarda

caseStudy.context: The Gemida family needed a digital home — a place to preserve their genealogy, share events, and keep the family connected across distances. This project was personal: built for my own family, the Kaliwat ni Cresenciano ug Ricarda.
caseStudy.challenge: Designing a system that could handle complex family tree relationships, support multiple user roles (admin vs. family members), and provide an intuitive interface for users of varying technical skill levels.
caseStudy.process: Leveraged AI-assisted development tools (Bolt.new, Cursor) alongside traditional coding in VSCode to accelerate development. Built on Next.js App Router with Neon/Prisma for the database, Vercel for deployment. Designed the family tree visualization, event timeline, image upload system, and admin interface iteratively.
caseStudy.outcome: A fully functional family heritage platform with user authentication, interactive family tree visualization, event management with timeline view, image galleries, and an admin dashboard. Deployed and actively used by the Gemida family. This project is still under development and is continuously improving.
takeaways: Explored AI-assisted development workflows with Bolt.new and Cursor IDE
Designed complex data relationships for genealogy trees
Built for a real user base with diverse technical backgrounds
Balanced personal passion with professional execution

documentary.intro: From a weekend AI-generated prototype to a tested, hardened heritage platform — the thirteen-month build story, told from the git log. 61 commits · 20 merged PRs · 14 active days · 1 author.

chapters.title: The Weekend Prototype
chapters.narrative: The project begins not with a blank editor but with a prompt. A Bolt.new scaffold dumps 76 files and 14,187 lines into a fresh repository — Next.js, a login screen, admin pages, events, a timeline, and a GoJS family tree, all wired to mock data. Two follow-up commits add a member details panel and zoom/pan to the tree. PR #1 merges. It works — sort of.

chapters.title: The Long Pause
chapters.narrative: Five months of dormancy. The prototype sits on GitHub — a skeleton of mock data with no database, no real auth, and no path to production. Semester demands and other projects pull focus. Side projects don't die during pauses; they wait.

chapters.title: Rebuilding on Real Data
chapters.narrative: One intense day. The mock data dies. Admin pages get API-backed CRUD, the family tree gets a management surface, and image uploads arrive with loading states. Three PRs land the same day. The app stops being a demo and starts being a system.

chapters.title: Feature Buildout
chapters.narrative: Back-to-back sessions: user profile API, initial project docs, then event status with timeline sync and API validation on a dedicated feat-events-and-timeline branch, an admin members list with pagination via user-management, and GoJS refinements. By PR #9, the core feature surface — auth, family tree, events, timeline, admin, profile — exists.

chapters.title: Security & Identity
chapters.narrative: The turning point. First a security pass: auth secured, admin checks moved server-side, uploads hardened, Node runtime pinned for API routes. Then the repo grows a conscience — brand-identity, code-review, and anti-pattern agent skills; a full UI theming refactor; a WCAG contrast-audit script; and a data-model rename from relationship to gender with proper event subtypes. Thirteen commits in five days — the app gains both a lock and a face.

chapters.title: Going Responsive
chapters.narrative: A single PR reworks the responsive layout and adds mobile navigation. Families don't all gather around desktops.

chapters.title: The Second Pause
chapters.narrative: The same gravity as before — a pause, not an ending.

chapters.title: The Advisor Sprint
chapters.narrative: The project returns with a new discipline: numbered advisor branches, each named after a specific review finding. advisor/001 replaces broken localStorage auth with cookie-based requests. advisor/002 locks timeline mutations behind requireAdmin. Then the busiest day in the project's history — August 3: sixteen commits landing a rate-limit fix, Node runtime on the users route, a full Vitest API-integration suite (auth, events, family-members), an orphaned-events restore, a cascade-delete fix with test coverage, a verification baseline, and the merge of development into main. Nine advisor branches in all; the last, 009, sketches the next chapter — person detail pages and a gallery. The repository now has a test suite where there was none.

projects.title: 30-Day Blender Challenge
projects.tagline: 22 3D models created in 30 days — a journey of discipline and creative growth
projects.description: A self-imposed 30-day challenge to create one 3D model per day using Blender, building skills from simple objects to complex compositions.

caseStudy.context: After completing a DICT-sponsored 3D modeling training in 2021, I wanted to push my Blender skills further. I set myself a 30-day challenge: create one 3D model every day, starting simple and progressively tackling more complex subjects.
caseStudy.challenge: Maintaining creative momentum over 30 consecutive days while balancing other responsibilities. Each model needed to show growth — from basic shapes like rugs and cups to detailed objects like swords, game consoles, and architectural scenes.
caseStudy.process: Day 1 started with a simple rug. Each subsequent day introduced new techniques: UV mapping, material nodes, lighting setups, and mesh sculpting. Models progressed from everyday objects (cups, jars, candy canes) to more ambitious creations (Flavio's sword from Ang Panday, an ASUS ROG Phone replica, a house scene with a Christmas tree).
caseStudy.outcome: Completed 22 distinct 3D models, each viewable as interactive 3D objects on this portfolio. The challenge dramatically improved modeling speed, material understanding, and creative confidence in Blender.
takeaways: Consistency beats perfection — daily practice builds lasting skills
Progressive difficulty keeps creative challenges engaging
Documenting progress creates a compelling visual narrative

projects.title: Groze — Reality-Synced Grocery Tracker
projects.tagline: An offline-first Android app that tracks real-world prices and adapts to how you actually shop
projects.toolsUsed: Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, Room, Hilt, MVVM Architecture
projects.description: Groze is a realistic, adaptable grocery tracking app that helps users manage spending, track real-world prices, and shop smarter by acknowledging that plans change once you enter the store. Unlike standard checklist apps, Groze freezes your plan when you start shopping, then tracks every deviation — ensuring the app gets smarter with every trip.

caseStudy.context:
I built Groze to solve my own Note Overload. My Google Keep was filled with dozens of repetitive shopping lists, none of which talked to each other. I realized I was losing valuable information—specifically, price trends and product availability.

Groze replaces the "disposable list" workflow with a persistent, offline-first tracker. It’s designed for the power user who wants to know exactly what they spent last month, what they’re likely to spend today, and keep it all synced to the reality of the local shop floor.
caseStudy.challenge: Building an offline-first Android app with a complex state management system that can freeze a shopping plan, track real-time deviations (deltas), and sync updated prices back to a persistent item vault — all while keeping the UI responsive and intuitive.
caseStudy.process: Started with discovery and design adaptation from the iOS counterpart (Grock - by Ethan John Paguntalan), mapping screens to Material Design 3 guidelines. Built the foundational data layer with Room database for The Vault, implemented the cart planning and dynamic budget engine, then developed the Active Shopping Mode with plan-freeze and delta tracking. Using Jetpack Compose for reactive UI and Hilt for dependency injection.
caseStudy.outcome: Currently in active development with core features including The Vault (personal item repository), flexible cart planning, active shopping mode with plan-freeze, dynamic budget awareness, and finish trip summaries.
takeaways: Designed a 'Planning Freeze & Delta Tracking' system — the signature feature that separates Groze from standard grocery apps
Implemented offline-first architecture using Room database for persistent local storage
Applied MVVM architecture with Jetpack Compose for reactive, testable UI
Managed complex state transitions between planning, active shopping, and trip summary phases

documentary.intro: From an empty repository to a working, multi-currency grocery tracker in five working days — the Groze build story, told from the git log. 17 commits · 3 merged PRs · 5 active days · 1 author · ~7,356 insertions.

chapters.title: The Skeleton in a Day
chapters.narrative: One commit turns an empty repo into a running app: 53 files, 5,408 lines — Room schema v1 with three DAOs and entities, a Hilt database module, a navigation host with bottom bar, and the full screen set already in place (Vault, Trip Plan, Active Trip with its ad-hoc item and price-update sheets, Trip Summary, onboarding, and Plan/Shop/History tabs). The same day adds a settings screen with theme toggle and currency selection, a fix for the post-trip Vault-to-History redirect, and README/gitignore cleanup. PR #1 merges — the Android answer to the iOS Grock has a skeleton.

chapters.title: Painting It Dark
chapters.narrative: A full-screen pass the day after the skeleton lands: dark mode enabled across every screen — bottom bar, history, plan, shop, ad-hoc and price sheets — ripping out hardcoded colors (82 insertions, 124 deletions), then a redesign of the settings, trip management, and Vault screens with a new color palette (272 insertions, 200 deletions). The app stops looking like a scaffold and starts looking designed.
highlights: c6cb6d5 dark mode across all screens

chapters.title: Quantity, Debt & Docs
chapters.narrative: Cart items gain quantities across repository, screens, view models, and sheets (+261 lines) — PR #2 lands. Then a hard look at the app's biggest file: 115 insertions and 94 deletions paying down layout, typography, and UX debt in ActiveTripScreen. The README gains project-structure and database documentation. PR #3 merges to main — the last merge main would see for months.

chapters.title: Branding & the Goal Board
chapters.narrative: Two weeks pass; work resumes off main, on development. Launcher icons are rebuilt with new branding — play-store icon, adaptive foregrounds, five density buckets. Then the repo grows a written conscience: a GOAL.md state-tracker carrying the MVP checklist (onboarding, vault, cart planning, active shopping, trip summary, history — all checked), two named bugs (a finished trip that won't leave Active Shopping; a dead "add as new item" path), and five planned features including currency selection, dark mode, and category templates.

chapters.title: Beyond the Checkout Counter
chapters.narrative: The offline-first rule breaks — deliberately. A Retrofit service and Hilt network module bring live exchange rates; a repository with fallback rates keeps the app working when the network doesn't; CurrencyFormatter and CurrencyManager thread the chosen currency through nine screens and view models. 544 insertions in a single commit — the largest since the skeleton. It sits on development, unmerged.

chapters.title: The Quiet
chapters.narrative: Five and a half months of silence. development sits five commits ahead of main, unmerged; the goal board still lists its two open bugs. The README's status badge says in development, and that remains true — the project isn't abandoned, it's waiting for its next session.
